```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(mzLibR)
# Every call on this page is answered from a recording of the real bridge, made on the sample
# sheets and peptide tables this package ships in extdata/diff/, so the page builds anywhere. With
# a bridge installed, the same calls compute the answers.
.mzlibr_example <- mzLibR:::replay_bridge_start()
```

Before any differential test there are two tables to get right, and both are easy to get quietly
wrong. The **design**: which coefficient means what, which level is the baseline, whether two
things you want to separate can be separated by these samples at all. And the **observations**:
what each peptide measured in each biological sample, with fractions summed and technical
replicates averaged correctly, and a missing value kept as missing rather than written as 0.

`diff_design()` turns the sample sheet you already keep into mzLib's design matrix, which equals
R's `model.matrix()`, and says which comparisons cannot be estimated and why. `diff_observations()`
turns a FlashLFQ or MetaMorpheus peptide table into every peptide in every sample, as a log2
intensity or `NA` with the reason. Both write files that `stats_fit()` reads.

| question | function | mzLib | method |
|---|---|---|---|
| what is my design matrix, and which comparisons can these samples answer? | `diff_design()` | `AnalysisDesign.ByStratum`, `.DefaultContrasts`, `.Estimability` (#1450) | treatment coding as R's `model.matrix()` (Wilkinson and Rogers 1973) |
| what did each peptide measure in each sample, and if nothing, why? | `diff_observations()` | `FlashLfqObservations.FromPeptideTable`, `ObservationTable` (#1455) | fractions summed, technical replicates averaged in log2 |
| how far apart do the samples sit on the peptides they share? | `diff_observations()` | `SharedPeptideNormalization.Measure`, `.Apply` | median of ratios to a geometric-mean reference (as Anders and Huber 2010) |

Then test with `stats_fit()`: it reads the design file and the contrasts file `diff_design()`
writes, and the responses file `diff_observations()` writes. See
`vignette("stats", package = "mzLibR")`.

## From a sample sheet to a design

The differential-abundance article analyses a MALAT1 dilution series - 27 runs at 500, 250 or
125 ng - with a hand-made design of 0/1 columns. Here is the same experiment as a scientist writes
it down: one row per run, and its load.

```{r}
diff_data <- system.file("extdata", "diff", package = "mzLibR")
stats_data <- system.file("extdata", "stats", package = "mzLibR")
sheet <- read.delim(file.path(diff_data, "malat_dilution_samples.tsv"))
head(sheet, 3)
table(sheet$malat_load)
```

Say which column is a factor and which level is the baseline. Everything else is mzLib's:

```{r}
design <- diff_design(file.path(diff_data, "malat_dilution_samples.tsv"),
                      factors = list(factor_spec("malat_load", "500ng")),
                      out = file.path(tempdir(), "malat_design"))
stratum <- design$strata[["all"]]
stratum$column_names
c(rank = stratum$rank, aliased = length(stratum$aliased_terms), warnings = length(stratum$warnings))
design$records[, c("contrast_id", "label", "estimability")]
design$records$fitted_weights
```

- **The columns** are named `factor=level`. The reference comes first and has no column; the other
  levels follow in ordinal (character) order, so `125ng` before `250ng`. That is R's
  `model.matrix()` with the same level order.
- **The default contrasts** are each level against the reference. Each is one design column here,
  so `fitted_weights` has a single 1.
- **`out`** wrote `design_1.tsv`, the design table `stats_fit()` reads, and `contrasts_1.tsv`,
  each estimable contrast's weights on the same columns, which `stats_fit(contrasts = )` reads.

Fit it. Each contrast against the reference is its design column, tested by name:

```{r}
responses <- file.path(stats_data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv")
fit <- stats_fit(responses, stratum$design_file, c("malat_load=250ng", "malat_load=125ng"))
fit$status_counts
malat <- fit$records[fit$records$status == "fitted" & startsWith(fit$records$feature, "MALAT1:"), ]
aggregate(estimate ~ coefficient, data = malat, FUN = median)
```

The same numbers as the hand-made design, because it is the same model: this package's live tests
hold the two fits equal, feature by feature.

**Or test the contrasts file itself**, and get a confidence interval with each answer. Name the
coefficients too, and one call returns both tables:

```{r}
both <- stats_fit(responses, stratum$design_file, c("malat_load=250ng", "malat_load=125ng"),
                  contrasts = stratum$contrasts_file)
both$contrasts$weights
c2 <- both$contrasts$records[both$contrasts$records$contrast == "c2", ]
coefficient <- both$records[both$records$coefficient == "malat_load=250ng", ]
identical(c2$t, coefficient$t)
row <- c2[c2$status == "fitted" & startsWith(c2$feature, "MALAT1:"), ][1, ]
row[, c("feature", "observed", "estimate", "confidence_low", "confidence_high")]
```

A contrast of one column is that column's test, number for number, so `c2` repeats the
`malat_load=250ng` rows and adds the interval. This oligo was measured in 4 runs, and its 95%
interval cannot tell halving from no change. The contrasts file earns its keep for comparisons that
are no single column, such as 250 ng against 125 ng: declare no reference level and
`diff_design()` writes every pair, as the differential-abundance article shows.

## Covariates, units and batch

A covariate is a number in a unit. Say the unit, and how the slope should read: here age in years,
as a slope per decade, centred at 50 years. Batch is a fixed block. The sheet is mzLib's own test
design, and base R's `model.matrix()` for it ships beside it:

```{r}
design <- diff_design(file.path(diff_data, "design_factor_batch_covariate_samples.tsv"),
                      factors = list(factor_spec("condition", "ctrl")),
                      covariates = list(covariate_spec("age", "years", scale = 10, scaled_unit = "decade",
                                                       centre = 50)),
                      batch = "batch")
stratum <- design$strata[[1]]
stratum$column_names
design$records[2, c("label", "covariate_unit", "covariate_scale")]
r_matrix <- as.matrix(read.delim(file.path(diff_data, "design_factor_batch_covariate_matrix.tsv"),
                                 check.names = FALSE))
colnames(r_matrix)
max(abs(unname(stratum$matrix) - unname(r_matrix)))
```

Every value equals R's `model.matrix(~ condition + batch + I((age - 50)/10))`; this package's tests
also run `model.matrix()` here and compare.

**Leave a field out and mzLib chooses.** `covariate_spec("age", "years")` sends no scale, scaled
unit or centre, so the slope is per year and the centre is the stratum's mean;
`covariate_centres` reports the centre used. Batch enters the model only when you name its column,
and drops out with a warning in a stratum that has only one batch.

## When the samples cannot answer

Here every sample of condition A ran in batch 1 and every sample of B in batch 2:

```{r}
design <- diff_design(file.path(diff_data, "design_confounded_samples.tsv"),
                      factors = list(factor_spec("condition", "A")), batch = "batch")
stratum <- design$strata[[1]]
stratum$column_names
c(rank = stratum$rank)
stratum$aliased_terms
design$records[, c("label", "estimability")]
is.null(design$records$fitted_weights[[1]])
```

**No analysis of these samples can separate the condition from the batch**, and mzLib says so
instead of returning a number. The verdicts are `"estimable"`; `"not_estimable:confounded"`, where
the comparison lies along a direction two or more terms share, as here; and
`"not_estimable:rank_deficient"`, where it needs a column no sample informs, such as an
interaction cell with no samples.

The design file still holds a design that can be fitted: `fitted_column_names` leaves out the later
of two aliased columns, because a fit refuses a design without full rank. A contrast that is not
estimable has no fitted weights (`NULL`), so it never reaches the contrasts file.

## Strata: one design per tissue

When samples are different kinds of thing - liver and muscle - a comparison is made within each
kind. Name the stratum column, and each stratum gets its own design:

```{r}
design <- diff_design(file.path(diff_data, "stratified_samples.tsv"),
                      factors = list(factor_spec("condition", "A")), strata = "organism part")
lapply(design$strata, function(s) s$sample_ids)
design$strata[["organism part=kidney"]]$not_run
design$records[, c("stratum", "contrast_id", "label")]
```

Kidney has only condition A, so there is nothing to compare there, and `not_run` says so. **A
contrast id is numbered within its stratum:** `c1` is liver's first comparison and muscle's first,
so match strata by `label`. With `out`, stratum *i* writes `design_i.tsv`, numbered in the order of
`strata`, because a stratum key can hold characters a file name cannot.

## From a peptide table to observations

`diff_observations()` reads the peptide table FlashLFQ (`QuantifiedPeptides.tsv`) or MetaMorpheus
(`AllQuantifiedPeptides.tsv`) wrote, and needs the runs: which biological sample each file belongs
to and, if it applies, its fraction and technical replicate. **Grouping comes only from what you
give here**; mzLib never reads it out of a file name. This MetaMorpheus table is mzLib's test data:
three peptides in 18 runs, each run its own sample:

```{r}
peptides <- file.path(diff_data, "MetaMorpheus_1.1.11_AllQuantifiedPeptides.tsv")
groups <- file.path(diff_data, "MetaMorpheus_1.1.11_AllQuantifiedProteinGroups.tsv")
header <- strsplit(readLines(peptides, n = 1), "\t")[[1]]
files <- sub("-calib$", "", sub("^Intensity_", "", header[startsWith(header, "Intensity_")]))
head(files, 2)
runs <- data.frame(file = files, sample = files)
observed <- diff_observations(peptides, runs, basis = "mbr_kept", protein_groups = groups)
observed
```

MetaMorpheus quantifies calibrated files, so its columns end in `-calib`; give the file name without
it, and mzLib matches either. Each row is one peptide in one sample:

```{r}
transferred <- observed$records[observed$records$state == "mbr_transferred", ]
transferred[, c("base_sequence", "sample", "log2_intensity", "unique_protein_group")]
observed$records$state[is.na(observed$records$log2_intensity)][1]
```

**`basis` decides whether match-between-runs values count**, and mzLib has no default: it is your
scientific choice. Under `"msms_only"` the same cell has no value, and still says why:

```{r}
only <- diff_observations(peptides, runs, basis = "msms_only", protein_groups = groups)
same <- only$records[only$records$sample == "QE-002118_GM6_a" & only$records$base_sequence == "CACASHVAK", ]
same[, c("log2_intensity", "state")]
```

The protein-group table adds each group's q-value and flags. It is how a contaminant is recognised,
and mzLib warns about groups the peptides name that it does not describe:

```{r}
observed$protein_groups[observed$protein_groups$is_contaminant | observed$protein_groups$is_decoy, c("name", "genes")]
observed$warnings
```

What each `state` means:

- `quantified`: a value from MS/MS-identified peaks only.
- `mbr_transferred`: the value includes a match-between-runs peak. Under `"msms_only"` it is left
  out, and `log2_intensity` is `NA`.
- `ambiguous_peak`: a peak was found but withheld as ambiguous. No value.
- `identified_not_quantified`: identified by MS/MS, but no peak could be quantified. No value.
- `not_detected`: no value.

A sample whose runs disagree takes the most informative state among them. With fractions, mzLib
sums a technical replicate's fractions on the linear scale, then averages the sample's replicates in
log2: give `runs` `fraction` and `technical_replicate` columns.

## Normalization, and the assumption it makes

`diff_observations()` always measures how far each sample sits from the others, and subtracts it
only when you ask. mzLib's rule: over the peptides with a value in every sample (decoys,
contaminants and entrapments excluded), each sample's shift is the median of its log2 value minus
the peptide's mean. Two runs of FlashLFQ's E. coli spike-in vignette, which their names say were
spiked at 1x and 2x:

```{r}
spike_table <- file.path(diff_data, "EcoliSpikeIn_QuantifiedPeptides.tsv")
spike_runs <- data.frame(file = c("09-04-18_EcoliSpikeInSingleShot1x", "09-04-18_EcoliSpikeInSingleShot2x"),
                         sample = c("spike_1x", "spike_2x"))
spike <- diff_observations(spike_table, spike_runs, basis = "msms_only")
spike$normalization[c("setting", "reference_set_size")]
spike$normalization$warnings
```

**Below mzLib's floor of 100 shared peptides, nothing is shifted**, because a median of a few
peptides can move a whole sample by itself. You can lower the floor with `min_peptides`. Here is
what that does on this table:

```{r}
shifted <- diff_observations(spike_table, spike_runs, basis = "msms_only", min_peptides = 50,
                             normalize = TRUE, responses_out = file.path(tempdir(), "spike_in_responses.tsv"))
shifted$normalization$setting
round(shifted$normalization$shifts, 2)
by_peptide <- split(spike$records$log2_intensity, spike$records$full_sequence)
both_runs <- Filter(function(v) !anyNA(v), by_peptide)
c(peptides = length(both_runs), median_2x_minus_1x = round(median(sapply(both_runs, diff)), 2))
```

**The normalization removed the spike-in.** This slice of the vignette holds almost only E. coli
peptides, so nearly every peptide was doubled. The peptides measured in both runs sit close to one
log2 unit higher in the 2x run, the doubling the names promise, and the two shifts take all of it
away. Median normalization assumes most peptides do not change between samples. When most of them
do - a table of the spiked organism alone, a loading series, a pull-down - that assumption is false,
and normalizing deletes the result. **Read the shifts before you subtract them.**

`responses_out` also wrote the table's own peptide-by-sample shape, which `stats_fit()` reads as
its responses:

```{r}
shifted$responses_written[c("row_count", "sample_count")]
```

Its rows are peptides by full sequence, its columns the samples, and an empty cell means no value.
For more than one stratum, narrow `diff_observations()` to one stratum's samples with `samples` (a
design file from `diff_design()` will do): the shifts are measured over every sample of the table,
so measure each stratum on its own.

## What these functions will not do

- **No protein roll-up and no row choice.** mzLib does not yet turn the observation table into a
  protein-by-sample table, choose which rows a test uses (decoys, contaminants and q-value cuts
  included), or assemble fits into its differential result table. mzLibR does not do it either.
  Every peptide is a row; filter with `protein_groups`, `unique_protein_group` and the result's
  `protein_groups` table.
- **Only the default contrasts.** `diff_design()` lists each level against its reference (every
  pair when there is none) and each covariate's slope. mzLib's custom contrasts have no wire form
  yet; write your own contrasts file for `stats_fit()` instead.
- **The peptide table does not record FlashLFQ's design**, so mzLib cannot check that your runs
  group the files as FlashLFQ did. Give the runs the design FlashLFQ quantified with.
- **A table written in a comma-decimal locale does not read correctly.** FlashLFQ writes in the
  machine's culture, and mzLib reads with a decimal point.
- **mzLibR does no arithmetic.** Every number on this page came from mzLib.

## What to cite

The methods and resources behind the functions on this page, from their specs:

<!-- BEGIN cite: generated by scripts/render-cite.R from the verb specs; do not edit -->

- [doi:10.2307/2346786](https://doi.org/10.2307/2346786): the model-formula notation (main effects and a:b interactions) that R's stats::model.matrix implements and mzLib's design matrix equals (Wilkinson and Rogers, Appl Stat 22:392, 1973).
- [doi:10.1021/acs.jproteome.7b00608](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jproteome.7b00608): FlashLFQ, whose peptide table and detection types this verb reads (Millikin et al., J Proteome Res 2018).
- [doi:10.1186/gb-2010-11-10-r106](https://doi.org/10.1186/gb-2010-11-10-r106): the median-of-ratios idea the shared-peptide normalization follows: each sample against the log of a geometric-mean reference (Anders and Huber, Genome Biol 11:R106, 2010).
